The whole part's resale value
The whole shop's address only
content.explanation: Recording who calibrated, when, with what block and settings supports traceability and later verification.
distractors: The instrument color is not part of a calibration record.
Resale value is irrelevant to a calibration record.
An address alone does not document who calibrated and when.

content.stem: Which statement about calibration is correct?
options: Calibrate distance and sensitivity using known reference standards, verify it periodically, and record it
The whole calibration is only ever really needed just one single time ever here, somehow really quite oddly
Just any old scrap metal is always a fully valid standard here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed now
The whole gain alone is the entire whole calibration here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed now
content.explanation: Calibration sets the distance scale and sensitivity using controlled reference standards, is verified at intervals and on changes, and is recorded for traceability.
distractors: Calibration is verified repeatedly, not once ever.
Controlled, traceable standards are required, not scrap.
Calibration covers distance and sensitivity, not gain alone.

content.stem: Straight-beam (normal-incidence) testing usually uses a:
options: Longitudinal wave directed perpendicular into the part
A plain refracted shear wave here, somehow really quite oddly
A plain surface wave here, somehow really quite oddly
A plain radio wave here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Straight-beam work sends a longitudinal wave straight into the part, well suited to thickness and laminar (parallel-to-surface) reflectors.
distractors: Refracted shear waves are used in angle-beam work.
Surface waves follow the surface, not straight in.
Radio waves are not ultrasonic.

content.stem: In straight-beam thickness measurement, the key echo is the:
options: Backwall echo from the far surface
The whole initial pulse only here now
The plain whole couplant echo here now
The plain whole cable reflection here now
content.explanation: The backwall echo time, with the material velocity, gives the thickness. Its position moves with thickness changes.
distractors: The initial pulse marks entry, not thickness.
A couplant echo is not the thickness reference.
Cable reflections are not the thickness measurement.

content.stem: Thickness is computed from:
options: Half the round-trip time multiplied by the material velocity
The full round-trip time fully multiplied by the velocity here now
The echo amplitude fully multiplied by the gain here, oddly
The whole frequency fully divided by the velocity here, oddly
content.explanation: Sound travels to the back surface and back, so thickness equals half the round-trip time times velocity.
distractors: The round trip covers twice the thickness, so half the time is used.
Amplitude and gain do not determine thickness; time and velocity do.
Frequency divided by velocity gives a wavelength-related value, not thickness.

content.stem: Several equally spaced echoes on a thin part are typically:
options: Multiple backwall reflections
Several whole separate flaws here
Plain couplant signals here now
Plain whole cable noise here now
content.explanation: Sound bouncing between the two surfaces gives evenly spaced backwall multiples, which the technician recognizes rather than counting as flaws.
distractors: Equally spaced repeats are backwall multiples, not separate flaws.
They are backwall echoes, not couplant signals.
They are not cable noise.

content.stem: A lamination in plate often shows as:
options: A mid-wall echo with reduced or lost backwall
A much stronger whole backwall here, somehow oddly
No change at all here, somehow really quite
A plain color band here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: A lamination parallel to the surface reflects sound at mid-wall and can repeat, while the true backwall weakens or disappears.
distractors: A lamination reduces, not strengthens, the backwall.
A lamination does change the display.
It is an echo, not a color band.

content.stem: Straight-beam testing is best at finding reflectors that are:
options: Parallel to the surface, such as laminations
Perpendicular to the surface, such as vertical cracks
Only on the surface
Only magnetic
content.explanation: A straight beam reflects strongly off reflectors facing it (parallel to the surface). Reflectors perpendicular to the surface often need angle-beam work.
distractors: Perpendicular cracks are better found with angle beams.
Straight beam reaches internal reflectors, not only the surface.
UT detects acoustic reflectors, not magnetic ones.

content.stem: A tight crack perpendicular to the surface may be missed by a straight beam because it:
options: Reflects little sound back to the transducer
Speeds the whole sound up as it passes here
Is too small for any frequency to detect
Lies fully below the whole backwall here right now
content.explanation: A crack edge-on to a straight beam returns little energy, so angle-beam inspection is used to direct sound across such flaws.
distractors: The issue is reflection geometry; the crack does not speed the sound up.
The crack is missed due to orientation, not because no frequency could detect it.
A through-wall vertical crack is within the thickness, not below the backwall.

content.stem: For thin walls or corroded surfaces, a good choice is a:
options: Dual-element transducer
Large single low-frequency probe only
Magnet
Film cassette
content.explanation: Dual-element probes reduce the dead zone and handle rough, corroded, or thin walls well, common in corrosion thickness work.
distractors: A large low-frequency single probe is not ideal for thin, corroded walls.
A magnet is not a UT transducer.
A film cassette belongs to radiography.

content.stem: Measuring very thin material with a single straight probe is limited by the:
options: Dead zone near the surface
Backwall being far too strong
Couplant being far too thin
Cable being far too short
content.explanation: Near-surface echoes can fall in the dead zone of a single probe, so dual-element or delay-line probes are used for thin material.
distractors: A strong backwall is not the limiting factor for thin material.
Couplant thickness is not the dead-zone cause.
Cable length is not the dead-zone cause.

content.stem: On a small-diameter pipe, straight-beam coupling is improved with a:
options: Contoured shoe or proper technique to match the curve
A flat probe forced right down hard here, somehow
A plain magnet here, somehow really quite oddly enough
A plain dry contact here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Matching the probe to the curved surface improves coupling and beam entry, giving more reliable readings than a flat probe rocking on the curve.
distractors: Forcing a flat probe on a curve couples poorly.
A magnet is not used for coupling.
Dry contact leaves a sound-blocking air gap.

content.stem: A digital thickness gauge displays:
options: A numerical thickness value
The whole part's hardness here
The whole refracted beam angle
The whole couplant viscosity
content.explanation: Dedicated thickness gauges show a numeric reading (some also show a waveform), calibrated to the material velocity.
distractors: Hardness is measured by a different instrument, not a thickness gauge.
Refracted angle is an angle-beam setup value, not a thickness-gauge readout.
Couplant viscosity is not displayed by a thickness gauge.

content.stem: An incorrect velocity setting in a thickness gauge will:
options: Give an incorrect thickness reading
Have no real effect at all here now
Fully change the whole couplant here
Fully magnetize the whole part here now
content.explanation: Thickness scales with velocity, so a wrong velocity yields a wrong thickness even when coupling and echoes are good.
distractors: Velocity errors do affect the reading.
Velocity setting does not change the couplant.
Velocity setting does not magnetize the part.

content.stem: To measure metal thickness through a coating, an echo-to-echo mode helps by:
options: Measuring between two backwall echoes to ignore the coating
Adding the whole coating right to the reading here, somehow oddly
Removing the whole metal echo here, somehow really quite
Coloring the whole display here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Echo-to-echo measures the interval between successive backwall echoes, which represents the metal and excludes the coating layer.
distractors: Echo-to-echo excludes, rather than adds, the coating.
It uses the metal backwall echoes; it does not remove them.
It does not color the display.

content.stem: If the backwall echo disappears during scanning, the technician should:
options: Investigate for a flaw, lamination, or coupling loss
Just assume the whole part is fully perfect here, oddly
Just stop the recording here, somehow really oddly
Greatly increase the whole velocity here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: A lost backwall can mean a large reflector, lamination, heavy attenuation, or lost coupling, all of which the technician checks.
distractors: A lost backwall is a reason to investigate, not to assume perfection.
Recording continues; the condition is investigated.
Changing velocity does not explain a lost backwall.

content.stem: When scanning an area for thickness or laminations, the technician should:
options: Overlap passes to cover the whole area
Just skip the whole large gaps here now
Inspect just a single whole point here
Just avoid the whole edges here right now
content.explanation: Overlapping passes ensure full coverage so thinning or laminations are not missed between scan lines.
distractors: Gaps can leave thinning or flaws undetected.
A single point is not full coverage.
Edges are included in the coverage.

content.stem: Scanning too fast can:
options: Cause small indications to be missed
Greatly improve the whole coverage here
Greatly increase the velocity here
Fully magnetize the whole part here
content.explanation: Excessive scan speed can skip over small reflectors or thinning, so a controlled speed is used per the procedure.
distractors: Fast scanning hurts, not helps, coverage.
Scan speed does not change material velocity.
Scan speed does not magnetize the part.

content.stem: During straight-beam scanning, a maintained backwall echo helps confirm:
options: Adequate coupling and sound transmission
The exact whole flaw size here right now
The whole acceptance result here right now
The whole refracted angle here right now
content.explanation: A steady backwall indicates the sound is entering and returning, a quick check that coupling is adequate as the technician scans.
distractors: A backwall echo confirms coupling, not the size of any flaw.
It indicates sound is passing, not an accept or reject decision.
Refracted angle relates to angle-beam setup, not the straight-beam backwall.

content.stem: Recording thickness readings across a grid to find thinning is called:
options: Corrosion mapping or thickness surveying
Plain magnetizing here, somehow quite oddly
Plain whole film interpretation here now
Plain whole penetrant dwell here right now
content.explanation: Taking and recording readings on a grid maps remaining wall thickness to locate corrosion or erosion thinning.
distractors: Magnetizing is unrelated to thickness surveying.
Film interpretation belongs to radiography.
Penetrant dwell belongs to PT.

content.stem: Very thin sections are challenging because the echoes:
options: Crowd near the initial pulse and can overlap
Spread fully far apart here, somehow oddly
Disappear right into the whole cable here now
Fully change color here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: As thickness drops, backwall echoes move close to the initial pulse and can merge, so dual-element or high-frequency delay-line probes are used.
distractors: Thin-section echoes crowd together, not spread apart.
The echoes are in the part, not the cable.
It is a timing issue, not a color change.

content.stem: Before thickness gauging on a rough or scaled surface, the technician should:
options: Prepare the surface enough for good coupling
Leave loose scale right in place here right now
Add plain thick paint here, somehow oddly
Skip the whole cleaning always here now too
content.explanation: Loose scale and roughness scatter sound and disrupt coupling, so the surface is cleaned or conditioned enough for reliable readings.
distractors: Loose scale disrupts coupling and readings.
Thick paint can bias readings unless accounted for.
Some preparation is needed on poor surfaces.

content.stem: Laminations are well detected by straight beam because they are usually:
options: Oriented parallel to the plate surface
Perpendicular to the whole surface here
On the whole edge only here right now
Plain magnetic here, somehow quite oddly
content.explanation: Rolling produces laminations parallel to the surface, which face a straight beam and reflect strongly.
distractors: Perpendicular reflectors are harder for a straight beam.
Laminations are within the plate, not only at the edge.
Detection is acoustic, not magnetic.

content.stem: For consistent straight-beam readings, the couplant film should be:
options: Thin and consistent
Thick and variable here
Fully absent now
Replaced by the air
content.explanation: A thin, consistent couplant film gives stable coupling and repeatable readings; thick, varying films can shift results.
distractors: Thick, variable films reduce repeatability.
Some couplant is required.
Air does not couple sound into the part.

content.stem: A good practice for an important thickness reading is to:
options: Take repeat readings and confirm coupling and calibration
Just take one single reading and then move on here, oddly
Increase the whole gain until any number appears here, oddly
Just ignore the whole backwall here, somehow really oddly
content.explanation: Repeating readings and confirming coupling and calibration guards against a one-off coupling or setup error.
distractors: A single reading may hide a coupling error.
Forcing a number with high gain is not valid measurement.
The backwall is central to the measurement.

content.stem: In thin parts, extra small echoes between backwall multiples may be from:
options: Mode-converted or geometry signals the technician must recognize
Just real cracks in every single case here, somehow really
Just a fully drained battery here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Excessive couplant viscosity here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Mode conversion and geometry can add small echoes; the technician recognizes them rather than assuming each is a flaw.
distractors: Such echoes are not cracks in every case; they are often mode conversion or geometry.
A drained battery would not create these specific extra echoes.
Couplant viscosity does not create mode-converted echoes.

content.stem: Compared with a flaw detector, a basic thickness gauge is optimized to:
options: Report wall thickness quickly
Build the whole DAC curves here
Do the angle-beam weld sizing
Fully expose the whole film here now
content.explanation: Thickness gauges are streamlined for fast, accurate wall readings; full flaw detectors offer the A-scan and controls for flaw work.
distractors: DAC building is a flaw-detector task.
Angle-beam weld sizing is a flaw-detector and higher-level task.
Film exposure belongs to radiography.

content.stem: Thickness readings should be recorded with:
options: Their locations and the relevant settings
No identifying whole location here right now
Only the whole ambient temperature here
Only the whole instrument color here right now
content.explanation: Recording where each reading was taken and the setup supports mapping, comparison over time, and traceability.
distractors: Readings without locations lose much of their value.
Temperature alone does not identify where the reading was taken.
The instrument color is not useful record content.

content.stem: Switching from steel to a different alloy for thickness gauging requires:
options: Setting the correct velocity for the new material
No real change to the whole setup here, oddly
A much higher whole pulse repetition rate here
A much larger whole transducer only here right now
content.explanation: Each material has its own velocity, so the gauge is set to the correct value before measuring the new material.
distractors: A different material has a different velocity, so a change is required.
Pulse repetition rate does not correct for a different material velocity.
Probe size alone does not address the velocity difference.

content.stem: On hot piping, thickness readings can be affected by temperature, so the technician:
options: Uses high-temperature gear and applies any required correction
Just fully ignores the temperature here, somehow really quite oddly
Just uses plain ice on the probe here, somehow really quite
Just fully turns off the gauge here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: High-temperature probes and couplants and a temperature correction keep hot-service readings valid.
distractors: Temperature can bias readings and is not ignored.
Icing the probe is not the proper method.
Turning off the gauge does not take a reading.

content.stem: For lamination checks on plate before welding, the technician scans:
options: The area to be welded and adjacent zones per procedure
Just one single random spot here, somehow really
Only ever the whole plate edge here, somehow really quite
Just nothing at all here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Scanning the weld-prep area and adjacent material per the procedure ensures laminations that could affect the weld are found.
distractors: A single random spot is not adequate coverage.
Only the edge misses interior laminations.
The check must actually be performed.

content.stem: In straight-beam and thickness work, the Level I technician:
options: Takes and records readings and indications under direction
Fully sets the whole remaining-life criteria here, oddly
Fully approves the whole inspection plan here, somehow oddly
Fully dispositions the whole component here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: A Level I performs measurements and records results; setting criteria, approving plans, and dispositioning are higher-level responsibilities.
distractors: Remaining-life criteria are set above the Level I.
Approving the plan is above the Level I.
Component disposition is above the Level I scope.

content.stem: A sudden very low thickness reading should be:
options: Verified for coupling, peak jumping, and an interim reflector before accepting
Just recorded without any check at all here, somehow really quite oddly
Just assumed to be plain paint here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here
Just fully ignored here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here right now
content.explanation: Spurious low readings can come from poor coupling, peak jumping to an earlier signal, or the gauge locking onto a mid-wall reflector such as a lamination, so the technician verifies before recording a critical value.
distractors: A critical reading is verified, not recorded blindly.
It should be checked, not assumed to be paint.
An anomalous reading is investigated, not ignored.

content.stem: Which statement about straight-beam and thickness work is correct?
options: A straight longitudinal beam measures thickness from the backwall and finds laminar reflectors
The whole straight beam is always the very best for the vertical cracks here, somehow really quite
The whole velocity setting does not matter at all here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed now
The whole coupling does not affect the readings here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Straight-beam UT uses the backwall echo and velocity to measure thickness and is well suited to laminar reflectors, with correct velocity and consistent coupling essential.
distractors: Vertical cracks usually need angle-beam inspection.
Velocity setting directly affects thickness readings.
Coupling strongly affects readings.

content.stem: Angle-beam inspection in steel typically introduces a:
options: Refracted shear wave at a known angle
A plain straight longitudinal wave here
Just a whole surface wave only here now
Just a plain whole radio wave here now
content.explanation: A wedge refracts and mode-converts the sound so a shear wave travels into the part at a known angle, used for welds and similar geometries.
distractors: A straight longitudinal wave is straight-beam, not angle-beam.
Surface waves are a different mode for surface flaws.
Radio waves are not ultrasonic.

content.stem: The beam index point is the location where the:
options: Sound beam exits the wedge into the part
The whole cable connects right up here now
The whole couplant is poured here now
The whole backwall fully ends here now
content.explanation: The beam index point (exit point) is where the beam leaves the wedge; distances to reflectors are measured from it.
distractors: The cable connection is not the beam index point.
Couplant location is not the beam index point.
The backwall is the far surface, not the exit point.

content.stem: The refracted angle is used along with sound path to determine a reflector's:
options: Surface distance and depth
Just its outer color here
Just its whole weight here
Just its magnetism here, oddly
content.explanation: Knowing the angle and the sound path lets the technician compute how far along the surface and how deep a reflector lies.
distractors: The angle is not used to find color.
It is not used to find weight.
It is not used to find magnetism.

content.stem: In angle-beam work, a leg is the portion of the sound path:
options: Between reflections off the surfaces (for example first leg to the backwall)
Down in the whole cable here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here right
In the whole couplant here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here
Fully outside the whole part here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here
content.explanation: The beam travels in legs, reflecting between the surfaces. The first leg reaches the far surface; the second leg continues after that reflection.
distractors: A leg is in the part, not the cable.
A leg is in the part, not the couplant.
Legs are within the part, not outside it.

content.stem: The skip distance relates to the angle and the part thickness and describes the:
options: Surface distance for the beam to complete a full V-path
The whole depth of the first reflector here, somehow oddly
The whole thickness of the wedge here, somehow oddly
The whole width of the transducer element here, oddly
content.explanation: Skip distance is the surface distance over which the beam goes down and back up (a full V), used to plan transducer positions for full coverage.
distractors: Skip distance is a surface distance, not the depth of a reflector.
The wedge thickness is not the skip distance.
Element width is not the skip distance.

content.stem: Inspecting a weld, the technician uses first-leg and second-leg positions to:
options: Cover the weld volume from root to cap
Inspect only the whole weld cap surface
Measure the whole part thickness only
Set the whole reject level here now
content.explanation: Moving the probe toward and away from the weld places the beam at different legs so the full cross-section, root through cap, is examined.
distractors: Using both legs covers the full volume, not only the cap surface.
Leg positions are for coverage, not just thickness measurement.
Reject level is an instrument setting, not the purpose of leg positions.

content.stem: To evaluate a reflector with an angle beam, the technician:
options: Manipulates the probe to maximize the echo, then notes its position
Just uses the first echo seen without ever moving here, somehow
Just lowers the gain to fully hide it here, somehow really quite oddly
Just fully removes the couplant here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Rotating and moving the probe to peak the signal gives the best response and helps locate the reflector accurately.
distractors: Peaking the signal by movement is needed, not just the first glimpse.
Hiding the indication defeats the inspection.
Removing couplant loses the signal.

content.stem: A common angle-beam weld scanning motion combines:
options: Advancing along the weld while moving toward and away from it
Just a single straight line only here, somehow really quite
Just holding the whole probe still here, somehow really quite oddly
Just scanning only the whole cap here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: The technician advances along the weld while oscillating toward and away, often with rotation, to cover the volume and catch various flaw orientations.
distractors: A single straight line misses much of the volume.
Holding still does not scan the weld.
Only scanning the cap misses the root and body.

content.stem: Welds are typically scanned with the angle beam from:
options: Both sides and in both directions where access allows
Just one single side only here, somehow really quite oddly
Only the whole cap surface here, somehow really
Only inside the whole pipe here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Scanning from both sides and directions improves the chance of crossing flaws of different orientations and covering the whole weld.
distractors: One side may miss flaws favoring the other direction.
Cap-only scanning is not full coverage.
Access permitting, both surfaces and sides are used.

content.stem: Transfer correction in angle-beam work adjusts for differences between the calibration block and the part in:
options: Surface roughness and attenuation
The whole weld length here right now
Only the ambient temperature here
The transducer serial number here now
content.explanation: When the part surface and attenuation differ from the block, a transfer correction keeps the sensitivity reference valid on the part.
distractors: Weld length is not what transfer correction addresses.
Ambient temperature alone is not the basis for transfer correction.
The transducer serial number does not affect the sensitivity transfer.

content.stem: In weld scanning, echoes from the root, cap, or counterbore are:
options: Geometry signals the technician must recognize, not automatically flaws
Always plain rejectable flaws here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed
Just plain couplant echoes here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed now
Just plain cable noise here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed
content.explanation: Weld geometry produces predictable echoes; the technician learns to recognize these so they are not confused with flaw indications.
distractors: Geometry echoes are not automatically flaws.
They are weld-geometry echoes, not couplant echoes.
They are not cable noise.

content.stem: The points where the angle beam reflects off a surface are sometimes called:
options: Nodes (skip points)
The couplant points here
The plain cable nodes
The plain color points
content.explanation: Node or skip points are where the beam meets a surface and reflects; knowing their locations helps plan coverage and interpret signals.
distractors: They are beam reflection points, not couplant points.
They are not cable nodes.
They are not color points.

content.stem: Before angle-beam scanning, the technician:
options: Verifies the index point, angle, distance, and sensitivity
Just skips the whole calibration to save time here, oddly
Only ever checks the whole battery level here, somehow oddly
Only ever records the whole part color here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Angle-beam setup confirms the beam index point, refracted angle, distance calibration, and reference sensitivity before inspection.
distractors: Calibration is required before scanning, not skipped.
Battery level alone is not the angle-beam setup.
Part color is not part of the angle-beam setup.

content.stem: As an angle-beam wedge wears, the technician should expect the:
options: Index point and refracted angle to shift, requiring recheck
The whole frequency to fully double here, somehow really quite
The couplant to change its color here, somehow really
The whole cable to fully lengthen here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Wedge wear moves the exit point and can change the refracted angle, so these are rechecked periodically and after heavy use.
distractors: Wedge wear does not double the frequency.
It does not change couplant color.
It does not lengthen the cable.

content.stem: From the sound path and refracted angle, the surface distance to a reflector is found using the:
options: Geometry of the angle (a trigonometric relationship)
Just the whole echo amplitude alone here, somehow oddly
Just the pulse repetition rate here, somehow oddly
Just the whole couplant viscosity here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Surface distance and depth follow from the sound path and angle by trigonometry, which the technician applies or reads from a calculator or chart.
distractors: Amplitude does not give the surface distance; the angle geometry does.
Pulse repetition rate is unrelated to locating the reflector.
Couplant viscosity does not determine surface distance.

content.stem: A reflector found in the second leg is located by accounting for the:
options: Reflection off the far surface (using the skip geometry)
Just the whole initial pulse amplitude here, somehow oddly
Just the whole transducer frequency here, somehow really oddly
Just the whole couplant viscosity here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Second-leg reflectors are above the far surface in the return path, so the depth is computed from the skip geometry, not read as a simple first-leg depth.
distractors: The initial pulse amplitude does not locate a second-leg reflector.
Frequency does not change the second-leg geometry.
Couplant viscosity is unrelated to the second-leg location.

content.stem: Different refracted angles are used to:
options: Better intersect flaws of different orientations and weld bevels
Just increase the whole battery life here, somehow really quite oddly
Just shorten the whole cable here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Lower the whole pulse repetition rate here, somehow really
content.explanation: Choosing 45, 60, or 70 degrees helps the beam strike flaws and fusion faces more squarely depending on the joint geometry.
distractors: Angle choice does not affect battery life.
Angle choice does not change the cable.
Angle choice is about flaw orientation, not pulse repetition rate.

content.stem: Angle-beam scanning needs couplant that:
options: Maintains coupling as the probe moves over the surface
Just dries fully instantly here, somehow really quite oddly
Is fully unnecessary here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Is fully replaced by the air here, somehow really
content.explanation: A suitable couplant maintains a consistent film as the probe is manipulated, keeping sensitivity stable during scanning.
distractors: Instant drying would break coupling during scanning.
Couplant is required for contact angle-beam work.
Air does not couple the sound.

content.stem: Mode-converted or geometry echoes during angle-beam scanning can:
options: Appear as indications the technician must correctly identify
Never ever appear in any single setup here, somehow really quite
Appear only ever in the straight-beam testing here, oddly
Always be much stronger than the real flaws here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Angle-beam work can show mode-converted and geometry signals; recognizing them prevents false calls and missed real flaws.
distractors: Such echoes do appear and must be recognized.
They occur in angle-beam work, not only straight-beam.
They are not always stronger than real flaw echoes.

content.stem: When an angle-beam indication is found, the technician records its:
options: Position, sound path, and amplitude relative to reference
Just its outer color here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Just its whole weight here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Just its magnetism here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Recording where the indication is, its sound path or depth, and its amplitude versus reference supports later evaluation.
distractors: Color is not recorded for a UT indication.
Weight is not the recorded quantity.
Magnetism is not the recorded quantity.

content.stem: Angle-beam scan passes should overlap to:
options: Ensure the full weld volume is covered
Just save the whole couplant here now
Just reduce the whole coverage here now
Just avoid the whole root here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Overlapping passes prevent gaps so the entire weld cross-section is examined.
distractors: Overlap is about coverage, not saving couplant.
Overlap increases, not reduces, coverage.
The root must be covered, not avoided.

content.stem: A straight beam is often inadequate for weld cracks because the cracks are:
options: Frequently oriented so a straight beam reflects little from them
Always fully parallel to the whole surface here, somehow really
Always right on the whole surface here, somehow really quite oddly
Plain magnetic here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here
content.explanation: Many weld flaws are oriented such that a straight beam misses them, so an angled shear beam is directed to strike them more squarely.
distractors: Weld cracks are not always parallel to the surface.
Weld flaws are not always at the surface.
Detection is acoustic, not magnetic.

content.stem: Angle-beam sensitivity is commonly set using:
options: Side-drilled holes or notches in a reference block
The whole part's own backwall only here, oddly
The whole initial pulse height here, somehow oddly
Plain random surface reflectors here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Side-drilled holes and notches provide repeatable reflectors at known depths to set angle-beam reference sensitivity, sometimes forming a DAC.
distractors: The part's backwall alone is not the angle-beam sensitivity reference.
Initial pulse height is not used to set angle-beam sensitivity.
Known reference reflectors are used, not random surface reflectors.

content.stem: During a long angle-beam job, sensitivity and calibration are:
options: Rechecked at intervals and after changes
Set once and then never rechecked here
Fully ignored here, somehow really quite oddly
Changed fully at random here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Periodic rechecks and rechecks after probe, cable, or temperature changes keep the inspection valid.
distractors: A single setup is not enough for a long job.
Calibration is not ignored.
Settings are controlled, not random.

content.stem: Good angle-beam coverage requires the scanning surface to be:
options: Prepared so the probe couples and moves smoothly
Heavily scaled here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Coated very thickly with the whole paint here
Fully irrelevant here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: A reasonably clean, smooth surface lets the probe couple and slide for consistent angle-beam scanning.
distractors: Heavy scale disrupts coupling and movement.
Thick paint can disrupt coupling and beam entry.
Surface condition does matter.

content.stem: After locating and recording an angle-beam indication, evaluation against acceptance criteria is:
options: Generally a Level II or III responsibility
Fully performed by the Level I alone here
Fully skipped entirely here, somehow oddly
Based only on the whole loudest echo here now
content.explanation: A Level I detects, locates, and records; sizing and accepting or rejecting against the code is normally a higher-level task.
distractors: Acceptance evaluation is above the Level I scope.
Evaluation is required, not skipped.
Acceptance is judged against criteria, not simply the loudest echo.

content.stem: On pipe welds, a contoured wedge is used so the angle beam:
options: Couples and enters at the intended angle on the curved surface
Just skips the whole weld here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Just becomes a straight beam here, somehow really quite oddly enough
Just needs no calibration here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: A wedge contoured to the pipe maintains coupling and the intended refracted angle on the curved surface.
distractors: The goal is to inspect, not skip, the weld.
It remains an angle beam, not a straight beam.
Calibration is still required.

content.stem: Marking skip distances on the part helps the technician:
options: Position the probe for first-leg and second-leg coverage
Change the whole material velocity here, somehow oddly
Increase the whole transducer frequency here, somehow oddly
Reduce the whole part thickness here, somehow quite oddly
content.explanation: Reference marks for skip distances guide probe placement so the weld is covered in the appropriate legs.
distractors: Marking distances does not change the material velocity.
It does not change the transducer frequency.
It does not change the part thickness.

content.stem: An angle-beam indication's significance is first gauged by comparing its amplitude with the:
options: Reference level (for example DAC or a set percent of screen)
Just the whole initial pulse height here, somehow really quite
Just the whole scanning speed used here, somehow really quite oddly
Just the whole transducer serial number here, somehow
content.explanation: Indications are compared with the reference sensitivity (such as a DAC curve or set screen height) to decide what is recorded and passed for evaluation.
distractors: The initial pulse height is not the evaluation reference.
Scanning speed affects coverage, not the amplitude reference.
The transducer serial number is not a reference level.

content.stem: In angle-beam scanning, the Level I technician:
options: Scans, locates, and records indications under direction
Fully sizes and dispositions the flaws right to code here
Fully approves the whole procedure here, somehow oddly
Fully sets the whole acceptance criteria here, oddly
content.explanation: A Level I performs the scanning and records indications; sizing, disposition, procedure approval, and criteria are higher-level functions.
distractors: Sizing and disposition to code are above the Level I.
Approving procedures is above the Level I.
Setting acceptance criteria is above the Level I.

content.stem: To help judge whether an angle-beam echo is from a real reflector, the technician can:
options: Move the probe and observe how the signal behaves with position
Just assume every single echo is a flaw here, somehow really quite
Just turn off the whole instrument here, somehow really quite
Just fully ignore the whole probe position here, somehow really oddly
content.explanation: How a signal moves and changes with probe position helps distinguish real reflectors from geometry or spurious signals, before evaluation.
distractors: Not every echo is a flaw; behavior is assessed.
Turning off the instrument does not assess the signal.
Probe position is key to interpreting the signal.

content.stem: Which statement about angle-beam scanning is correct?
options: A refracted shear beam covers the weld in legs, with reflectors located from sound path and angle
The whole angle beam just uses a plain straight longitudinal wave here, somehow really quite oddly
The whole geometry never ever causes any echoes here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed now
The whole Level I just sizes the flaws right to code here, somehow really quite oddly enough now
content.explanation: Angle-beam UT uses a refracted shear wave, covers welds in first and second legs, and locates reflectors from sound path and angle, with evaluation left to higher levels.
distractors: Angle beam uses a refracted shear wave, not a straight longitudinal wave.
Weld geometry does cause recognizable echoes.
Sizing flaws to code is above the Level I scope.

content.stem: When an indication is found, the Level I technician records its:
options: Location, amplitude, and sound path or depth
Just its outer color here, somehow really quite
Just its whole weight here, somehow really quite
Just its magnetism here, somehow really
content.explanation: Recording where the indication is, how strong it is versus reference, and its depth or sound path supports later evaluation and traceability.
distractors: Color is not a UT indication parameter.
Weight is not recorded for a UT indication.
Magnetism is not recorded for a UT indication.

content.stem: A UT record typically identifies the part, procedure, equipment, settings, technician, and:
options: Date and calibration details
The weather conditions
The transducer's resale value
The shop's phone number only
content.explanation: Capturing the date and calibration details ties the results to a known setup and supports traceability and repeatability.
distractors: Weather is not the needed identifying detail for a UT record.
Resale value is irrelevant to a UT record.
A phone number alone does not document the date and calibration.

content.stem: Vertical (amplitude) linearity checks confirm the display responds:
options: Proportionally to changes in echo amplitude
Only ever to the color here, somehow really quite
Only ever to the couplant here, somehow
Fully randomly here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Vertical linearity verifies that screen height changes in proportion to input amplitude, so amplitude-based evaluation is valid.
distractors: Linearity is about amplitude response, not color.
It is not about couplant.
A linear display responds proportionally, not randomly.

content.stem: Horizontal (distance) linearity checks confirm that:
options: Screen positions correspond accurately to sound path or depth
The whole echo amplitude fully doubles with the gain here
The whole battery is fully charged here, somehow really quite oddly
The couplant is the right color here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Horizontal linearity verifies the sweep represents distance accurately, so reflector positions and thickness are correct.
distractors: Amplitude response is vertical linearity, not horizontal.
Battery charge is not what horizontal linearity verifies.
Couplant color is unrelated to distance linearity.

content.stem: Instrument linearity checks are:
options: Performed at required intervals, sometimes by the Level I under direction
Never ever done here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here right now
Only plain marketing here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here
Done by the whole part supplier here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed
content.explanation: Linearity is checked on a schedule to keep the instrument valid; a Level I may perform routine checks and record them under direction.
distractors: Linearity checks are required, not skipped.
They are a real performance check, not marketing.
They are done by qualified personnel, not the part supplier.

content.stem: Calibration verification intervals during inspection exist to:
options: Catch drift before it invalidates results
Slow down the whole work for no real reason
Fully replace the whole procedure here
Fully set the whole acceptance criteria
content.explanation: Periodic verification catches setup drift so readings stay valid, with reinspection of affected items if a check fails.
distractors: The purpose is validity, not arbitrary delay.
Verification supports, not replaces, the procedure.
It does not set acceptance criteria.

content.stem: Consistent couplant use is a process control because changes can:
options: Shift signal amplitude and affect readings
Fully change the whole part color here now
Fully magnetize the whole part here now
Fully expose the whole film here right now too
content.explanation: Because coupling affects amplitude, consistent couplant and technique between calibration and inspection keep results valid.
distractors: Couplant does not change the part color.
Couplant does not magnetize the part.
Couplant does not expose film.

content.stem: Surface temperature is controlled in UT because it can affect:
options: Couplant performance and sound velocity
The whole part's magnetic properties here
The whole transducer serial number
The whole instrument's color here now
content.explanation: Temperature changes velocity and can degrade standard couplants, so limits and high-temperature gear are used as required.
distractors: Temperature control here concerns coupling and velocity, not magnetism.
The serial number is unaffected by temperature.
The instrument color is irrelevant to temperature control.

content.stem: A safety characteristic of UT is that it:
options: Produces no ionizing radiation
Emits strong gamma rays here
Requires a radiation area here
Needs the whole film badges here
content.explanation: UT uses sound and emits no ionizing radiation, avoiding the radiation hazards and controls of radiography.
distractors: UT does not emit gamma rays.
UT does not require a radiation area.
Film badges are a radiography control, not needed for UT sound.

content.stem: In immersion UT, a key safety consideration is:
options: Electrical safety around water and equipment
Plain whole radiation shielding here right now
Plain explosive gases always here right now
Plain whole magnetic fields here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Combining water with electrical equipment requires proper grounding, GFCI protection, and care to prevent shock hazards.
distractors: Immersion UT does not involve ionizing radiation shielding.
Explosive gas is not an inherent immersion-UT hazard.
Strong magnetic fields are not the immersion-UT hazard.

content.stem: Automated scanning equipment introduces hazards such as:
options: Moving parts and pinch points
Plain ionizing radiation here
Plain penetrant fumes here now
Plain magnetizing current here now
content.explanation: Scanners and manipulators have moving parts, so guarding and awareness prevent pinch and entanglement injuries.
distractors: UT scanning does not involve ionizing radiation.
Penetrant fumes belong to PT.
Magnetizing current belongs to magnetic particle testing.

content.stem: Spilled couplant on the floor is a:
options: Slip hazard that should be cleaned up
A fully required condition here now
A plain whole magnetizing aid here now
A plain radiation source here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Couplant spills are slippery; cleaning them up and managing waste maintain a safe, orderly work area.
distractors: A spill is a hazard, not a requirement.
Couplant is not a magnetizing aid.
Couplant is not a radiation source.

content.stem: The Level I technician performs UT according to:
options: The written procedure and instructions
Plain personal preference each time here
Just whatever is the fastest here now
Plain memory of a whole different job
content.explanation: Work follows the qualified written procedure so results are valid and repeatable, with questions referred to higher-level personnel.
distractors: Personal preference is not the basis for the method.
Speed does not override the procedure.
A different job's memory does not govern this inspection.

content.stem: Inspection results should be reported:
options: Accurately and completely to the responsible personnel
Only ever verbally with no record at all here, oddly
Fully altered so the whole part passes here, somehow oddly
Summarized as a plain simple pass with no data here
content.explanation: Accurate, complete records are provided to the responsible parties; results are never altered, and data is retained per requirements.
distractors: A verbal-only report leaves no traceable record.
Altering results to pass is falsification.
A bare pass with no data does not support traceability or review.

content.stem: UT personnel typically must meet a vision requirement for:
options: Near vision, to read the display and records
Color only, with no near vision at all here
No whole vision requirement at all here now
Plain distance vision only here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Reading the display and documentation requires adequate near vision, verified per the written practice and rechecked periodically.
distractors: Near vision is required, beyond color alone.
Vision requirements do apply to NDT personnel.
Near vision, not only distance vision, is relevant.

content.stem: If a reading looks unfavorable, the technician should:
options: Record it accurately and refer evaluation to the proper level
Just change it to look fully acceptable here, somehow really
Just delete it here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here
Just round it to pass here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed
content.explanation: Data is recorded truthfully; evaluation against criteria is done by qualified personnel. Altering data is falsification.
distractors: Changing data to look acceptable is falsification.
Deleting unfavorable data is improper.
Rounding to pass is falsification.

content.stem: Recording the gain, reference level, and probe used allows the inspection to be:
options: Repeated and verified later
Charged to the customer twice
Completed without any probe
Run at any random sensitivity
content.explanation: Documenting the setup supports repeating and verifying the inspection and comparing results over time.
distractors: Recording settings supports repeatability, not billing.
A probe is required; records do not remove that need.
The point of recording settings is consistent, not random, sensitivity.

content.stem: When an indication needs sizing or acceptance decisions, the Level I:
options: Refers it to a Level II or III
Decides the acceptance alone here
Fully ignores it all here now
Removes it from the whole record
content.explanation: Sizing and acceptance are higher-level tasks, so the Level I records the indication and refers it for evaluation.
distractors: Acceptance decisions are above the Level I.
Indications are referred, not ignored.
Indications are kept in the record, not removed.

content.stem: Routine equipment and calibration checks should be:
options: Recorded so the instrument's validity is documented
Done fully without any record at all here, oddly
Fully skipped just to save the time here, oddly
Fully estimated from plain memory here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Recording checks documents that the instrument was valid during the work, supporting traceability.
distractors: Undocumented checks leave validity unproven.
Skipping checks risks invalid results.
Memory is not a substitute for recorded checks.

content.stem: Appropriate UT safety practice includes:
options: Following site PPE and electrical and mechanical safety rules
Just fully ignoring all the site rules here, somehow really quite
Just removing all the machine guards here, somehow really quite
Working in the restricted areas without any clearance here
content.explanation: UT work follows general site safety, including PPE, electrical safety (especially immersion), and machine guarding around scanners.
distractors: Site rules are followed, not ignored.
Guards stay in place for safety.
Restricted areas require proper clearance.

content.stem: UT records are generally:
options: Retained per the applicable requirements
Thrown right away immediately here now
Kept only ever if it is convenient here
Never ever created here, somehow quite oddly
content.explanation: Records are kept for the required retention period so results can be reviewed and verified later.
distractors: Records are retained, not discarded immediately.
Retention is a requirement, not a convenience.
Records are created as part of the inspection.

content.stem: Documenting settings and calibration supports repeatability, which means:
options: Another technician can reproduce the inspection and results
The whole results can never ever be checked here, somehow
Each single inspection is fully unique and unverifiable here
The whole data is fully hidden here, somehow really quite oddly
content.explanation: Repeatability lets the inspection be reproduced and verified, a core reason for thorough records.
distractors: Good records make results checkable, not uncheckable.
Documentation makes inspections verifiable, not unverifiable.
Records are shared with responsible parties, not hidden.

content.stem: If the instrument fails a linearity or calibration check, the technician should:
options: Stop, address the fault, and re-examine affected work
Just continue on and hope here, somehow really quite oddly
Just record nothing at all here, somehow really quite oddly
Just increase the gain and proceed here, somehow
content.explanation: A failed check means results may be invalid, so the cause is corrected and affected items are re-examined per procedure.
distractors: Continuing on a faulty instrument risks invalid results.
The failure and actions are documented, not omitted.
Raising gain does not fix a linearity or calibration fault.

content.stem: Couplant should be chosen so it is:
options: Compatible with the part and safe to handle
Fully corrosive right to the whole part here
Always fully flammable here, somehow oddly
Fully toxic by design here, somehow quite oddly
content.explanation: Couplant is selected to avoid harming the part (for example chloride limits on stainless) and to be safe to handle per its safety data sheet.
distractors: A corrosive couplant can damage the part.
Flammability is a hazard to avoid, not a goal.
Couplant is chosen to be safe, not toxic.

content.stem: On austenitic stainless steel, couplant is often controlled for:
options: Low halogen/chloride content to avoid harming the material
High chloride content on purpose here, somehow really
Plain bright color here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed
Plain magnetism here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed
content.explanation: Chlorides can harm stainless, so low-chloride couplants are specified for such materials per the procedure.
distractors: High chloride can damage stainless, so it is avoided.
Couplant color is not the control here.
Magnetism is not the couplant control.

content.stem: The scanning coverage and directions are:
options: Defined by the procedure and followed by the technician
Just chosen fully at random each time here, somehow oddly
Just skipped to save the time here, somehow really quite
Decided by the part's color here, somehow really oddly
content.explanation: The procedure defines coverage and scanning directions to ensure the required volume is examined, which the Level I follows.
distractors: Coverage is defined by the procedure, not random.
Coverage is not skipped for speed.
The part's color does not define scanning coverage.

content.stem: Professional and ethical practice in UT requires:
options: Honest, accurate recording and reporting of results
Fully adjusting the results just to please others here
Fully omitting the whole unfavorable findings here
Just guessing whenever you are fully unsure here
content.explanation: Integrity demands truthful records; when unsure, the technician refers to higher-level personnel rather than guessing or hiding data.
distractors: Adjusting results to please others is falsification.
Omitting findings is falsification.
Guessing is replaced by referring questions to higher levels.

content.stem: Overall, the Level I in UT is qualified to:
options: Set up, calibrate, scan, and record under direction
Independently interpret and accept right to code here
Fully approve the whole procedures here, somehow
Fully certify the personnel here, somehow really quite
content.explanation: A Level I performs the inspection and records results under direction; interpretation to code, procedure approval, and certification are higher-level functions.
distractors: Independent acceptance to code is above the Level I.
Approving procedures is above the Level I.
Certifying personnel is above the Level I scope.

content.stem: If the technician is unsure whether a signal is relevant, the best action is to:
options: Record it and consult higher-level personnel
Just erase it here, somehow really quite oddly
Just assume it is fully nothing here, oddly
Just pass the whole part here, somehow oddly
content.explanation: Uncertain signals are recorded and referred for evaluation rather than dismissed, keeping the inspection sound.
distractors: Erasing an uncertain signal risks missing a flaw.
Assuming it is nothing can miss a real flaw.
Passing the part is an acceptance decision above the Level I.

content.stem: Which statement about recording, control, and safety is correct?
options: Record results accurately, keep equipment verified, and follow electrical and mechanical safety
Just fully alter all the data so the whole part passes here, somehow really quite oddly enough now
Just fully skip all the equipment checks here, somehow really quite oddly enough indeed here
The whole UT just always requires the radiation shielding here, somehow really quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Sound UT practice records results honestly, keeps the instrument verified through linearity and calibration checks, and follows safety, including electrical care in immersion and guarding around scanners.
distractors: Altering data is falsification.
Equipment checks keep results valid and are not skipped.
UT uses sound and needs no radiation shielding.

content.stem: API 1104 allows ultrasonic testing of girth welds as:
options: A substitute that borrows the radiographic limits
A method that needs no calibration before scanning itself
A visual technique carried out along the weld
A permitted method with its own acceptance provisions
distractors: UT does not borrow RT limits.
UT requires calibration.
UT is not a visual method.
content.explanation: UT is an accepted method under API 1104 and carries acceptance provisions distinct from radiography.

content.stem: At Level I, an ultrasonic operator under API 1104 mainly:
options: Sets up, scans, and records the indications found
Signs off the final disposition of the weld
Writes the company's acceptance criteria for UT
Approves the welding procedure used on the joint itself
distractors: Disposition is a Level II/company step.
Criteria are set by the standard/company.
Procedure approval is separate.
content.explanation: Level I carries out the examination and records results; evaluation and disposition sit above Level I.

content.stem: Before scanning a weld, the UT instrument is calibrated on a:
options: A section taken from the production weld itself
A blank plate carrying no reflectors at all
A radiograph taken of the same girth joint
A reference standard with known reflectors
distractors: The production weld is not a calibration standard.
Calibration needs known reflectors.
A radiograph does not calibrate UT.
content.explanation: Calibration uses a reference block with defined reflectors to set range and sensitivity.

content.stem: Indications are recorded for evaluation when they reach the:
options: The reference (evaluation) level set at calibration
The film density threshold read on the shot
The operator's own preferred gain on the day as well
The end of the working shift on the spread
distractors: Density is radiographic.
Recording is not by preference.
Time of day is irrelevant.
content.explanation: Indications at or above the reference/evaluation level are recorded and assessed against the acceptance criteria.

content.stem: A reportable UT indication is sized chiefly by its:
options: Its color as displayed on the instrument screen
Its length measured along the line of the weld
Its distance from the stenciled pipe number
The volume of couplant used during the scan
distractors: Color is not measured.
Marking position is irrelevant.
Couplant amount is a setup detail.
content.explanation: Indication length is the primary size parameter for acceptance under the workmanship route.

content.stem: A transfer correction accounts for the difference in:
options: The film speed selected for the exposure
Surface and material attenuation between block and part
The source-to-film distance set for the shot on the joint
The developer temperature used in processing
distractors: Film speed is radiographic.
SFD is a radiographic geometry term.
Developer is radiographic.
content.explanation: Transfer correction adjusts for attenuation/coupling differences between the calibration block and the actual part.

content.stem: Welds are examined ultrasonically mainly with:
options: Straight-beam longitudinal waves only
Surface (Rayleigh) waves only along the cap as well
No transducer, reading the bare echo
Angle-beam shear waves aimed into the fusion faces
distractors: Straight beam alone misses the bevel.
Surface waves do not cover the volume.
A transducer is required.
content.explanation: Angle-beam (shear) probes interrogate the weld bevel and fusion faces where planar flaws lie.

content.stem: The scan is arranged so the beam covers:
options: The finished weld cap surface only
The root bead surface region only
The full weld volume and both fusion faces
The pipe body well away from the weld itself
distractors: Cap-only is incomplete.
Root-only is incomplete.
The body is not the target.
content.explanation: Scanning patterns ensure the beam sweeps the entire weld volume and fusion faces.

content.stem: Surface condition matters in UT because it affects:
options: Coupling, and so the sound that enters the part
The film density on the finished radiograph itself
The IQI placement chosen beside the weld
The exposure time used to shoot the joint
distractors: Density is radiographic.
IQIs are radiographic.
Exposure is radiographic.
content.explanation: Rough or fouled surfaces degrade coupling and can mask indications.

content.stem: A crack-like planar reflector found by UT is:
options: Acceptable when the reflector measures short
Rejectable wherever it is found in the weld
Acceptable when it sits below the weld cap
Ignored entirely on smaller diameter pipe
distractors: Length does not make a crack acceptable.
Location does not make it acceptable.
Pipe size is irrelevant.
content.explanation: Planar crack-like reflectors are rejectable.

content.stem: UT may be judged by alternative (ECA) criteria when they are:
options: Chosen by the operator running the scan
Needed to pass a weld that otherwise fails on the joint
Invoked by the company and supported by qualification
Used as a way to skip the calibration step
distractors: Operators do not select the route.
ECA is not a pass-through for failures.
Calibration is still required.
content.explanation: Alternative criteria apply only when the company invokes and qualifies them.

content.stem: UT calibration can be invalidated by a significant change in:
options: The ambient light level around the work area itself
Part temperature, which affects the sound velocity
The brand of film loaded for the shot
The color of the pipe being examined
distractors: Light does not change velocity.
Film is radiographic.
Color is irrelevant.
content.explanation: Temperature changes sound velocity and can shift the calibration.

content.stem: Indications meeting the threshold are:
options: Erased afterward to save on stored data
Recorded with their location and their length
Reported only verbally to the next hand
Left for the following shift to deal with itself
distractors: Data is retained, not erased.
Records are documented, not verbal only.
Recording is not deferred.
content.explanation: Reportable indications are documented with position and length for evaluation.

content.stem: A UT indication that exceeds the acceptance criteria is a:
options: Discontinuity found anywhere along the weld
Couplant trail left across the scan surface
Defect
Reference reflector used during calibration
distractors: A discontinuity may be acceptable.
A couplant trail is not an indication.
A reference reflector is a calibration target.
content.explanation: A discontinuity becomes a defect only when it exceeds the criteria and is rejectable.

content.stem: Calibration is rechecked during the job to confirm it has not:
options: Changed the grade of the pipe being examined itself
Altered the film loaded in the cassette
Drifted from the set range and the sensitivity
Moved the weld away from its marked position
distractors: UT does not change pipe grade.
No film is involved.
The weld does not move.
content.explanation: Periodic checks confirm range and sensitivity have not drifted.

content.stem: Acceptance or rejection of a UT-examined weld is decided by the:
options: The Level I operator running the instrument
The couplant supplier providing the gel
The company, using the acceptance criteria
The pipe mill that supplied the joint
distractors: Level I records, not dispositions.
Suppliers do not disposition.
The mill supplies pipe only.
content.explanation: The company dispositions the weld based on the criteria and the recorded results.

content.stem: A UT-rejected section after repair is:
options: Re-examined by the same method and criteria
Accepted on the strength of the repair note
Judged the second time by relaxed limits
Exempt from any re-test once repaired
distractors: A note is not re-inspection.
Limits do not relax.
Re-examination is required.
content.explanation: The repair is re-inspected to the same method and acceptance basis.

content.stem: UT is valued alongside radiography because it is strong at finding:
options: Only surface-breaking porosity along the cap itself
Film artifacts left during the processing
Coating defects on the outside of the pipe
Planar flaws such as lack of fusion and cracks
distractors: UT is not limited to surface porosity.
Film artifacts are radiographic.
Coating is not the target.
content.explanation: UT is well suited to vertically oriented planar flaws that radiography can miss.

content.stem: UT used to show API 1104 compliance is performed by personnel who are:
options: Qualified and certified for the UT method
Members of the welding crew on the spread
Chosen by lottery from the available hands
Approved by the coating crew on the line
distractors: Welders are not the NDT authority.
Qualification is not by chance.
Coaters do not certify UT.
content.explanation: Examinations are performed by qualified, certified UT personnel.
